text: Congress required an appropriate medical screening in emergency rooms. The court immediately faced a problem: the statute never explained what appropriate actually meant.
provenance: EMTALA requires an appropriate medical screening, but does not explain what constitutes one.

text: The opinion called appropriate one of the most wonderful weasel words in the dictionary, useful because nobody publicly argues for inappropriate treatment.
provenance: Appropriate is one of the most wonderful weasel words in the dictionary, and a great aid to the resolution of disputed issues in the drafting of legislation.

text: But the joke did not decide the case. The court still needed a legal test that hospitals and patients could understand.
provenance: Who, after all, can be found to stand up for inappropriate treatment or actions of any sort?

text: Its answer began with a real screening procedure reasonably designed to identify critical conditions in people who arrive with symptoms.
provenance: First: a participating hospital must afford an appropriate medical screening to all persons who come to its emergency room seeking medical assistance.

text: Then came the controlling comparison: patients presenting substantially similar complaints must receive that level of screening uniformly.
The essence, the court said, is that some procedure exists and that the hospital administers it even-handedly.
provenance: The essence of this requirement is that there be some screening procedure, and that it be administered even-handedly.

text: That does not turn federal law into a promise of excellent medicine. A hospital can examine everyone badly without violating this particular rule.
provenance: A hospital that examines you badly has not broken this law.

text: So appropriate was not defined as best. It was defined through procedure and sameness, returning us to the slippery word that opened the case.
provenance: The adjectival phrase, the court observed, is not self-defining.
